scope: Family-name/thar/classification manuscripts linked by explicit Cambridge cross-references and shared published references, investigated as the classification branch of the probable 1864 Trunk 2 / second large bundle / item 12 multilingual family.
central_claim: One classificatory problem survives across English machine-paper, Farsi machine-paper, Nepali handmade-paper and Urdu handmade-paper documentary states. Language does not select paper support, and the version family cannot be reduced to a local-source/European-derivative binary.

relation_strength_key.A: explicit copy/another-copy relation or especially close title/content duplicate
relation_strength_key.B: explicit catalogue cross-reference within same classificatory/family-name problem
relation_strength_key.C_BROADER_CONTEXT: explicit catalogue cross-reference to broader ethnographic context, not same document form
relation_strength_key.X: catalogue cross-reference whose modern descriptions are semantically mismatched; do not use as stemma edge without inspection

material_patterns: English fair-copy/classification states occur on machine-made paper (vol.6/1, vol.9/10).
Farsi family-name state can also occur on machine-made paper (vol.101/8), so machine support is not an English-language marker.
Nepali family-name/genealogy states occur on Nepali handmade paper (vol.56/2, vol.51/14, vol.58/1).
Urdu family-name state can remain on Nepali handmade paper (vol.103/18), so handmade support is not a Nepali-language marker.
Farsi can also occur on Nepali handmade paper (vol.96/14), showing variation even within one language.
The same classificatory operation therefore crosses support regimes in both directions.
source_control_rules: Do not force directional descent among B-strength nodes without handwriting/textual comparison.
Shared publication reference does not prove all manuscript nodes directly generated the printed state.
vol.57/2 is broader Khasa ethnography and should not be treated as a direct family-name copy solely because vol.101/8 cross-references it.
vol.22/9 is a catalogue-link anomaly: preserve it but exclude it from the direct micro-stemma until object inspection.
Farsi, Urdu, Nepali/Khas and historical Persian labels remain distinct until scripts/texts are physically controlled.
Machine-made is formation class, not secure production origin.
